slides.heading: The Rise of Humanoid Robots
slides.body: From science fiction to factory floors — how walking, thinking machines are reshaping our world

slides.heading: What Is a Humanoid Robot?
slides.body: A humanoid robot has a body shaped like a human — two arms, two legs, a torso, and a head. This form factor lets them use tools, navigate stairs, and operate in spaces designed for people, without requiring any special infrastructure.

slides.heading: The Big Players Racing Ahead
slides.body: Tesla's Optimus, Figure AI's Figure 02, Boston Dynamics' Atlas, and Agility Robotics' Digit are all competing to deploy commercial humanoids. Major automakers, logistics companies, and tech giants are pouring billions into this race.

slides.heading: AI Is the Missing Piece
slides.body: Earlier robots followed rigid pre-programmed paths. Modern humanoids use large language models and vision AI to understand instructions, adapt to new environments, and even learn from demonstrations — the same way humans do.

slides.heading: Real Jobs, Real Factories
slides.body: BMW, Amazon, and Foxconn are already piloting humanoid robots on production lines. They handle tasks like pick-and-place, assembly, and inspection — jobs too complex for traditional fixed-arm robots but too repetitive or hazardous for people.

slides.heading: The Hardware Challenge
slides.body: Building a humanoid is brutally hard. Motors must be powerful yet precise, batteries must last a full shift, and actuators must absorb the shock of walking on uneven ground. Getting all this into a human-sized package at scale drives most of the R&D cost.

slides.heading: Cost Trajectory: Why It Matters
slides.body: Early humanoids cost $100,000+, but analysts expect prices to fall below $30,000 by the end of the decade — cheaper than a year of human wages in many countries. That crossover point could trigger mass deployment across industries.

slides.heading: Safety, Ethics & Regulation
slides.body: Who is responsible when a robot injures a worker? How do we prevent misuse in military or surveillance contexts? Regulators worldwide are racing to draft safety standards and liability frameworks before humanoids become truly widespread.

slides.heading: Impact on the Workforce
slides.body: Humanoids will likely automate physically demanding and dangerous jobs first — construction, mining, logistics. This could reduce workplace injuries but also displace workers who lack alternatives. Economists are sharply divided on the net effect.

slides.heading: The Robot Era Is Here
slides.body: Humanoid robots are no longer a promise — they are prototypes walking the same floors as human workers today. How we design, deploy, and govern them will define the next chapter of both technology and society.
